newsitem.title: USA: Secondhand-smoke trial to be a first in the U.S.
newsitem.headline: Secondhand-smoke trial to be a first in the U.S.

text.p: Six years of preliminary skirmishing, including six weeks of jury picking, end on Monday when a mom-and-pop pair of lawyers lay out a landmark secondhand smoke case charging America's tobacco companies with conspiracy.
The questions to be resolved in Norma Broin et al vs Philip Morris et al, a class action on behalf of 60,000 non-smoking flight attendants, will be scientific and legal:
Does secondhand smoke cause tobacco-related diseases?
Did the U.S. tobacco industry, including some of America's wealthiest companies, conspire to hide secondhand smoke's dangers?

If a six-member jury, including a nurse nearing retirement and a young cable-television installer, goes against the tobacco industry, plaintiff lawyers Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt will ask for $5 billion or more in damages.
"The issues are mostly common sense," said Susan Rosenblatt.

But tobacco analysts and lawyers say the science underlying claims that secondhand smoke causes lung cancer, heart disease and other ailments is not nearly as established as the research connecting cigarette smoking with other health risks such as emphysema.
"The defence will argue there is no direct evidence that secondhand smoke causes disease," said tobacco industry analyst Martin Feldstein of Smith Barney.

Anti-tobacco activist Richard Daynard of the Tobacco Products Liability Project at Northeastern University said the Rosenblatts will have substantial studies, including one done by Harvard University, to prove their claims.

The Harvard at study, published in May, covered 10 years and reported a near doubling of the risk for heart attacks and coronary disease among 32,000 healthy women routinely exposed to secondhand smoke.
Dueling doctors, scientists and statisticians detailing population studies will testify for both sides, lawyers said.

Daynard said he expected tobacco industry lawyers, numbering a dozen or more during jury selection, to challenge witnesses for the flight attendants aggressively, with the hope of distracting the jurors.

"What the defendants sometimes do is object so often and have so many sidebars (private conferences with the judge) that they disrupt the continuity," Daynard said. "No jury can pay attention through that."

Beyond the science, the Rosenblatts must prove that Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco and seven other defendants knew the risks of secondhand smoke and conspired against Americans to hide the dangers.
Stanley Rosenblatt has said he will call two former U.S. surgeons general to testify, including one whose move to limit smoking in some public places was blunted during the 1970s.
He is also likely to use the videotaped questioning of top tobacco company executives done in recent months and industry documents used in other anti-tobacco trials.
Feldman said the jury composition of four men and two women, with only two of the jurors over 50 years old, would in traditional lawsuits by smokers have been favourable toward the tobacco companies.

"Young males tend to be more defensive of the industry than older females, who often tend to feel sympathy toward the plaintiffs," Feldman said. "But some of the traditional agruments about individual responsibility don't work in this case."

All the plaintiffs, including Norma Broin, a 42-year-old mother whose lung cancer is in remission, were non-smokers and claim their tobacco-related diseases were caused by passengers' cigarette smoke aboard U.S. jets before 1988. Smoking was banned on U.S. domestic flights in 1988.

Testimony in Dade County Court is expected to last eight weeks or longer before the jury will decide the Broin case, the first class-action claim against the tobacco industry and the first secondhand smoke case to come to trial in the United States.
